text: A 'deep fake' is defined as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful [1][60].

AI literacy means skills, knowledge, and understanding that enable providers, deployers, and affected persons to make an informed deployment of AI systems, while also gaining awareness about the opportunities and risks of AI and the possible harm it can cause [1][56]. Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to support the development of AI literacy for their staff and others involved with the operation and use of AI systems, considering their technical knowledge, experience, education, training, and the context of use [4][1].
A small mid-cap enterprise or SMC is defined as a small mid-cap enterprise as defined in point (2) of the Annex to Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 [14b].

A "substantial modification" means a change to an AI system after it has been placed on the market or put into service that was not foreseen or planned in the initial conformity assessment by the provider [1][23]. This modification is considered substantial if it affects the system's compliance with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, or if it results in a modification to the intended purpose for which the AI system was assessed [1][23].

The AI Office is the Commission's function responsible for contributing to the implementation, monitoring, and supervision of AI systems and general-purpose AI models, as well as AI governance [1][47]. It is also tasked with developing Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI [64(1)]. Furthermore, the AI Office shall be allocated adequate resources to effectively perform its duties and exercise its powers in relation to the enforcement of this Regulation [64(3)].

The AI Act does not apply to AI systems where they are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes [1]. Furthermore, the Regulation does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union, where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes [1].

AI systems released under free and open-source licences are not exempt from the regulation unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50 [1]. Specifically, the obligations set out in Article 53, paragraph 2, do not apply to providers of AI models released under a free and open-source licence that allows for access, usage, modification, and distribution of the model, and whose parameters, including the weights, the information on the model architecture, and the information on model usage, are made publicly available [3]. This exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risks [3].

Yes, an AI system or AI model specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development is not covered by this Regulation [1]. However, research, testing, or development activities regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service are not excluded from the Regulation, and such activities must be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law [2].

Yes, the AI Act applies to your company under certain conditions. It applies to providers and deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located in a third country, provided the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union [4(c)]. This scope includes providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems or general-purpose AI models in the Union, regardless of whether the providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country [4(a)].

Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to support the development of AI literacy for their staff and other persons involved in the operation and use of AI systems [1]. This support should take into account their technical knowledge, experience, education, and training, as well as the context in which the AI systems are to be used and the persons or groups on whom the AI systems are to be used [1]. This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy for any individual [1].

Natural persons to whom human oversight is assigned must be enabled to properly understand the high-risk AI system's capacities and limitations and monitor its operation to detect and address anomalies [2][4(a)]. They must also be aware of the tendency to rely on the system's output and be able to correctly interpret the output, taking into account available interpretation tools [2][4(b)][4(c)]. Furthermore, they must have the ability to decide whether to use the system, disregard, override, or reverse its output in any particular situation [2][4(d)]. They can also intervene in the system's operation or interrupt it through a 'stop' button or similar procedure to bring it to a safe state [2][4(e)].

The provider must keep a written machine readable, physical or electronically signed EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service [1]. Furthermore, the provider shall keep the EU declaration of conformity up-to-date as appropriate by drawing it up [4]. The authorised representative must also keep a copy of the EU declaration of conformity for a period of 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service [22].

The provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative must register themselves and their high-risk AI system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service, unless it is a high-risk AI system referred to in point 2 of Annex III [1]. If the AI system is not considered high-risk according to Article 6(3), the provider or authorised representative must also register themselves and the system in the EU database [2]. Furthermore, deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies or persons acting on their behalf must register themselves, select the system, and register its use in the EU database before putting a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III on the market or putting it into service [3].

Yes, deployers who are employers must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of a high-risk AI system before putting it into service or using it at the workplace [1]. This information must be provided where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on information of workers and their representatives [1].

Deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III must perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights if they are deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), with the exception of high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III [5].

A fundamental rights impact assessment for a high-risk AI system must include the measures to be taken in the case of the materialisation of those risks, such as arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms [3]. Additionally, deployers shall perform an assessment consisting of the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected by the system's use in the specific context [4].

Yes, deployers of high-risk AI systems that make decisions or assist in making decisions related to natural persons must inform those natural persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system [1][11].

If a provider considers an AI system referred to in Annex III not high-risk, they must document their assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service [1]. This provider will also be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2), and they must provide this documentation upon request from national competent authorities [1].

Yes, small and medium-sized enterprises, including start-ups, may comply with certain elements of the quality management system required by Article 17 in a simplified manner [1]. This simplification is available provided they do not have partner enterprises or linked enterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC [1]. The Commission is responsible for developing guidelines on the elements of the quality management system that can be complied with in a simplified manner for SMEs [1]. However, this simplification does not exempt operators from fulfilling any other requirements or obligations laid down in the Regulation [1].

The placing on the market, putting into service, or using AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace institutions is prohibited, except when the use of the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons [1(f)]. However, Article 50 states that deployers of an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system must inform the natural persons exposed to it of the system's operation and process personal data according to Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable [5]. Furthermore, Article 26 requires employers who are deployers of a high-risk AI system at the workplace to inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system [2(7)].

Yes, the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of AI systems for the evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups of persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics is prohibited [1(c)]. This prohibition applies if the social score leads to either or both of the following outcomes: detrimental or unfavourable treatment of certain natural persons or groups of persons in social contexts unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected, or detrimental or unfavourable treatment of certain natural persons or groups of persons that is unjustified or disproportionate to their social behaviour or its gravity [1(c)(i) and (ii)].

No, the placing on the market, putting into service for a specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage is prohibited [1].

The ban on placing on the market, putting into service, or using an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic images, videos, audio, or similar material of an identifiable natural person’s intimate parts or of an identifiable natural person engaged in sexually explicit activities without their freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and explicit consent is prohibited [1].

Yes, the use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes is permitted under certain conditions [1][2]. This use must be deployed only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual [1][3]. It must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions related to the use in accordance with national law, including temporal, geographic, and personal limitations [2]. Furthermore, the use is authorized only if the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment and registered the system in the EU database, although urgent cases may allow commencement without immediate registration [2].

If the use of a 'real-time' remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces is in a duly justified situation of urgency, it may be commenced without an authorisation [1]. However, if such authorisation is requested without undue delay, it must be requested at the latest within 24 hours [1].

An AI system that manipulates material in a way that does not increase the exposure of any depicted intimate parts or alter the nature of any depicted sexually explicit activities shall not constitute manipulation [1b]. Therefore, such an AI system shall not constitute manipulation [1b].

An AI system is considered high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or if the AI system itself is a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I [1][1]. Furthermore, the product whose safety component is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for placing it on the market or putting it into service under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I [1].

An AI system referred to in Annex III shall not be considered high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making [1]. This exemption applies if the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity, is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or is intended to perform a preparatory task for an assessment relevant to the use cases listed in Annex III [1]. However, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons [1].
The provided passages do not contain information about AI tools that detect cheating during exams.

No, software that only organises the logistics of a political campaign is not considered a high-risk AI system. This is because Article 1(8)(b) excludes AI systems to the output of which natural persons are not directly exposed, such as tools used to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view [1].

Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep the automatically generated logs to the extent they are under their control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless otherwise provided in applicable Union or national law, particularly Union law on the protection of personal data [1]. If a provider is a financial institution subject to requirements regarding internal governance, arrangements, or processes under Union financial services law, they must maintain these logs as part of the documentation kept under the relevant financial services law [1].

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep the logs automatically generated by that system to the extent they are under their control [1]. This retention period must be at least six months, unless otherwise provided by applicable Union or national law, especially concerning personal data [1]. If a deployer is a financial institution subject to requirements under Union financial services law, they must maintain these logs as part of the documentation kept under that relevant law [1].

The reporting timeline depends on the nature of the incident. Generally, the report must be made immediately after the provider establishes a causal link or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, and not later than 15 days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the serious incident [1][2]. If the death of a person occurs, the report must be provided immediately after establishing or suspecting a causal relationship, but not later than 10 days after becoming aware of the incident [2][4]. For a widespread infringement or a serious incident as defined in Article 3, point (49)(b), the report must be provided immediately, and not later than two days after becoming aware of that incident [4].

If a serious incident involving the death of a person occurs, the report must be provided immediately after the provider or deployer establishes, or as soon as they suspect, a causal relationship between the high-risk AI system and the serious incident [1]. This report must be made no later than 10 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer becomes aware of the serious incident [1].

Providers of AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must ensure that these persons are informed that they are interacting with an AI system [1]. This obligation does not apply if it is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant, and circumspect natural person, taking into account the circumstances and context of use [1].

If you deploy an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake, you must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated [1]. This obligation does not apply if the use is authorized by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute a criminal offense [1]. If the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional, or analogous work or programme, the transparency obligations are limited to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hinder the display or enjoyment of the work [1].

Providers of general-purpose AI models have several obligations. They must draw up, keep up-to-date, and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems who integrate the model, which must enable those providers to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and comply with their obligations [1][2]. Furthermore, they must draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, which must contain at a minimum the information set out in Annex XI for the AI Office and national competent authorities [2]. They also have obligations regarding copyright and related rights, including identifying and complying with reservations of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [4]. Finally, they must draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training the general-purpose AI model, following a template provided by the AI Office [5].

The Commission shall take several criteria into account when determining if a general-purpose AI model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those set out in Article 51(1), point (a) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. These criteria include the number of registered end-users [1], the quality or size of the data set, such as measured through tokens [2], and the number of parameters of the model [3]. Additionally, the Commission shall consider the benchmarks and evaluations of the model's capabilities, which involves looking at the number of tasks without additional training, its adaptability to learn new, distinct tasks, its level of autonomy and scalability, and the tools it has access to [4]. Finally, the Commission must consider the input and output modalities of the model, such as text to text (large language models), text to image, multi-modality, and the state of the art thresholds for determining high-impact capabilities for each modality, as well as the specific type of inputs and outputs (e.g., biological sequences) [5].
A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have a high impact on the internal market if it has been made available to at least 10,000 registered business users established in the Union [1(f)].

Yes, providers of general-purpose AI models must put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights [1]. This includes identifying and complying with a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, including through state-of-the-art technologies [1].

For SMEs, including start-ups, each fine referred to in Article 99 shall be up to the percentages or amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, whichever is lower [1]. For SMEs, the Member States shall take into account their interests and economic viability when imposing penalties [2]. Furthermore, in the case of SMEs, including start-ups, the specific interests and needs of the SME providers shall be taken into account when setting the fees for conformity assessment under Article 43, which includes reducing those fees proportionately to their size and market size [3].
The provided passages do not contain information about relief on AI Act fines for small mid-cap companies.

If a decision is taken by a deployer based on the output of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, and this decision produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects a person in a way that they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety, or fundamental rights, the affected person has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations [86(1)]. This right applies to affected persons subject to such a decision [86(1)]. However, this right does not apply to the use of AI systems for which exceptions from, or restrictions to, the obligation under that paragraph follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law [86(2)].

Member States must ensure that they establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at the national level, which shall be operational by 2 August 2027 [1]. This sandbox may also be established jointly with the competent authorities of other Member States [1].
The high-risk requirements apply to high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

For AI systems classified as high-risk AI systems in accordance with Article 6(1) related to products covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section B of Annex I, only Article 6(1), Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112 shall apply [1]. For high-risk AI systems related to products covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, only the derogations from the conformity assessment established in that Union harmonisation legislation shall apply [3]. Furthermore, for high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, the provider of the system shall follow the relevant conformity assessment procedure as required in accordance with the relevant Union harmonisation legislation [5].

The Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union [113]. It shall apply from 2 August 2026 [113]. However, different chapters apply from various dates, such as Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, applying from 2 December 2027 for high-risk AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III [113].

Yes, high-risk AI systems already on the market or put into service may have to comply with the Regulation under certain conditions [1][2]. Specifically, providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended for public authorities must comply with the requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation by 2 August 2030 [1][2]. Furthermore, high-risk AI systems that have already undergone a conformity assessment procedure must undergo a new one if there is a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is distributed or continues to be used [3][4].

A provider is defined as a term that includes a product manufacturer, deployer, authorised representative, importer, or distributor [4]. A deployer is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body using an AI system under its authority, except when the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity [1][4].

The maximum administrative fine for non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices referred to in Article 5 is up to EUR 35,000,000 or up to 7% of the undertaking's total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. For non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices, the maximum administrative fine on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies is up to EUR 1,500,000 [2]. Furthermore, non-compliance of an AI system with requirements or obligations other than those in Article 5 can result in administrative fines of up to EUR 750,000 [3].

The AI Act provides that access to AI regulatory sandboxes is free of charge for SMEs, which includes start-ups, without prejudice to exceptional costs that national competent authorities may recover in a fair and proportionate manner [2(d)].
